rv.q: A pretentious play that induces much head-scratching.

Unfortunately, this awkwardly plotted "tragicomedy," with its sketchy humor and one-dimensional characters, feels like a missed opportunity to deliver some timely satire regarding greed and privilege in the halls of power.
Ring Twice for Miranda is fantasy suffering from a case of insufficient imagination.

But although Alan Hruska's new play Ring Twice for Miranda , which just opened at City Center Stage II, trades in these compelling ideas, its impact is more like that of a wet noodle to your shin than a baseball bat to your temple.
Perhaps I'm just eccentric, but I found Ring Twice for Miranda had enough going for it to warrant recommending it.
The actors are all very good, and there are dramatic pleasures in Ring Twice for Miranda, but they don’t amount to more than a thoroughly capable sci-fi yarn.
The play raises important and enduring questions but does not have the dramatic strength to carry the weight of these rich questions.
The problem with Ring Twice for Miranda is what happens after that turning point.
It's almost as if this play does not know what it wants to be.
The plot is too slight to justify the length of the play.
Unfortunately, the play itself isn't as compelling as these production elements.
If good intentions were reason enough to skew a review to the positive, “Ring Twice for Miranda” would merit a rave.
The attempt is more interesting than the result, as the play lacks the tightness and synchronized drive needed to rise above good intentions.
It lacks substance, and the story line has no pulse.

cn.t: Critics find this dystopian tragicomedy an ambitious but muddled exercise in existentialism, praising its intriguing premise while faulting sluggish pacing, one-dimensional characters, and a fizzling mystery that never delivers on its initial promise.
